title: Why Garuda carries Vishnu
hookLine: why the snakes run from Garuda, and why the strongest bird faces Vishnu with folded hands
carry: vahana: garuda's strength bows to vishnu
last: RAMA IS VISHNU, AND GARUDA KNOWS.

lines: THE SNAKES DON'T FIGHT. THEY FLEE.
TWO SISTERS AND A HORSE'S TAIL.
A SON WHO FREES HIS MOTHER.
cards: The arrows that were snakes didn't fight Garuda. The moment his wind reached the shore, they fled. People who grew up with Indian tales know why.
They've heard it from grandparents, in comics, in temple carvings. It's a story about two sisters, a horse's tail, a cheat, and a son who will do anything to set his mother free.
Valmiki doesn't stop to tell it, so here it is.

teach.b: It's told in the Mahabharata's first book. Two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, are both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru is the mother of the serpents; Vinata is the mother of Garuda.

teach.h: THE CHEAT ON THE HORSE'S TAIL.
teach.b: The sisters bet on the color of a divine horse's tail, and the loser becomes the winner's servant. Kadru cheats: she has her serpent sons hang on the tail so it looks black.
Vinata loses, and becomes a servant to her sister and the snakes.

Her son Garuda asks the serpents what it will take to free his mother. Bring us the nectar of immortality, they say, from the gods. So Garuda storms heaven and wins the nectar, and he doesn't taste a drop himself.
On the way, Vishnu, pleased with him, offers him a gift, and Garuda in turn agrees to serve Vishnu, as the bird he rides and the emblem on his banner. He frees his mother.
That's why snakes and Garuda are enemies, and why Garuda carries Vishnu.
Every Hindu god has a vahana, a mount: Shiva's bull Nandi, Ganesha's mouse, Durga's lion. Garuda is Vishnu's.
That's why, in many Vishnu temples, a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands, the way a devotee does.
Think what that shows: the bird who stormed heaven for his mother, strong enough to scatter serpents at Lanka, kept forever in service, hands joined.
Many teachers read the vahana that way: the greatest strength bows. So when you see Garuda in a temple, or in a family shrine, you're looking at a picture of what strength is for.

how: Garuda's story from the Mahabharata's Adi Parva is often told to children, and in many Vishnu temples a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands.

games.q: you're Garuda, flying home with the gods' nectar of immortality to free your mother. what do you do with it?
o: drink some first; you earned it.
carry it to free her, without tasting a drop.
give it back and fight the serpents instead.
games.why: he doesn't taste it. Vishnu, pleased, offers him a gift, and Garuda becomes the bird who carries Vishnu.

practice: In many Vishnu temples, Garuda faces the shrine with his hands joined. Join yours the same way.

Bring to mind someone who, like Garuda, would cross anything for a person they love, and for a few slow breaths, offer them to God in thanks. If you don't pray, keep your hands joined and simply be glad they're in the world.

wordCard.voice: Garuda, the great bird who freed his mother from Kadru's serpents, then chose to carry Vishnu, and still faces him with folded hands.

orig.note: Sanskrit amṛta: the nectar of immortality, literally 'not dying', from a-, not, and mṛta, dead.
